rows.answer_preview: Hawaiians memorized where more than 200 stars rise and fall in the night sky to determine north, south, east, and west. They used these star positions at night to know if they were heading in the right direction toward different places in the world. Yes, according to the lesson content, ancient Hawaiian people had their own units of measurement such as kīkoʻo, pīʻā, anana, and anakahi. They used these to measure things like fish (e.g., a 6-inch ʻula pāpapa or a seven-foot ʻahi), fishing lines, spears, and nets based on the size of the object being measured. /  / Source: L3 Kiʻi Pōhaku (Grade 4–5).

Angles in acute, obtuse, right, and straight types are used to design *hale* structures. The frame of the *hale*, including posts, beams, and rafters that create sloped roofs, incorporates these specific angle measurements during planning and construction by Native Hawaiian architects. Students identify these angles within the architectural designs compared to Western-style homes. /  / Source: A Hale

Everyday Anakahi & Measure Hunt is a lesson where students learn Native Hawaiian units of measurement (anakahi) using different parts of the body. Students will also write an opinion piece about which anakahi they prefer to use, sort objects into categories based on size ranges, and think about what ancient Hawaiians measured versus things people measure today. /  / Source: Everyday Anakahi & Measure
